sources.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'

discussion.body: The number worth watching is the smaller one. Five per cent is a commitment; the extra two is an option the board holds. A fund whose size depends on the goodwill of the same board that governs the company is a different animal from one whose shares are irrevocably set aside.

Nobody else in this story is offering an institution at all. Elon Musk's reply on social media was to recommend giving the shares directly to the public, adding that this is what he will be doing. That is a destination with no mechanism attached — and "the public" is not an address you can post shares to.

Still, both versions have to name recipients, and Anthropic's list is the more revealing part. A jobs-market fund sits oddly beside an industry record in which companies around the world, primarily tech firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption. Treating that as something a foundation should address, rather than only as a triumph of efficiency, is a choice worth noticing.

items.title: Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund: 5% of Shares Now, Another 2% if the Board Says So
items.body:
Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good". The Claude developer says its proposed Public Benefit Fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market. It also says none of the shares held by the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations, in the US or overseas.

There is a second, looser figure attached. In a statement released on Sunday, Anthropic said the fund could receive another 2% of its shares at the board's discretion. The BBC reports the announcement comes as the company lays the ground for a potential stock market listing that could value it at more than $1tn (£750bn).

sources.title: ‘Capturing Bigfoot’ Review: An Astounding Documentary Uncovers the Truth

discussion.body: The promise is the story. A documentary that opens by announcing an old dispute is settled is really testing how badly the audience wants a clean ending.
But the critic’s description points away from a clean ending: the film is about how the legend was born and took hold, which makes the creature secondary to the believing.

The timing sharpens that. The critic frames the release against new “credibility” for belief in the uncanny from select U.S. military officials’ UAP testimony, and against older mythologies unmasked as hoaxes. A film saying “Until now” is selling certainty into a market that has been burned and is still shopping.

items.title: A 59-Second Bigfoot Film, and a Documentary That Promises ‘Until Now’
items.body: The famous Bigfoot footage runs 59 seconds. Variety’s critic dates it precisely: Roger Patterson shot it in Northern California on 20 October 1967. The documentary “Capturing Bigfoot” takes on the legend around that reel — how it was born, how it took hold, and how the iconic piece of film came to be. The critic calls it an astounding documentary. It also arrives with a provocative frame. An opening title, as the review describes it, says no one has ever been able to determine whether the film is real or a hoax. The next line is “Until now.” That is a more interesting promise than a yes-or-no verdict on one reel: the film can offer the truth and still be most revealing about the appetite for a final answer.

discussion.body: Which makes autumn a reveal rather than a repaint. The yellows and reds show through once the green production falls away, so the show is created by what the tree stops doing, not by what it starts doing.

Reveal is a generous word for it. Colder air and shorter days make the tree curtail production of the molecule it uses to synthesise food — that's a wind-down, and the colour is a side effect of the shutdown. Beautiful side effect, admittedly.

items.title: Autumn Comes to Bieszczady When the Beeches Stop Making Green
items.body:
On 8 October 2026, the Operational Land Imager on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite caught southeast Poland's Bieszczady National Park mid-transformation. European beech dominates the park's forests, with sycamore maple among the species adding to the autumn display — beech and other deciduous trees blanketing the hillsides starting to sport reds and golds.

The colour itself is subtraction. Dropping air temperatures and waning daylight cause these trees to curtail production of chlorophyll, the molecule plants use to synthesise food. As that production falls away, the leaves' green pigments fade, and the yellows and reds of other pigments show through. Which means the cue to stop making food is also the cue that lets the other colours appear: nothing needs to be painted on for the hillside to go gold.

sources.title: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness

discussion.body: Put those two figures next to each other — growth of 4.5% in the quarter, property investment down more than 20% over nine months — and they read like two different economies. One is picking up, the other is still going the wrong way, and nothing in the headline growth rate closes the gap between them.

A rebound from a three-year low is a modest bar to clear, and the lift is coming from AI-related export demand. That's the part with an asterisk: global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding the outlook, so a good quarter built on that demand is a good quarter partly rented from elsewhere.

items.title: China's Economy Picked Up to 4.5% as the AI Boom Helped Lift Exports
items.body:
China's economy grew 4.5% in the three months to the end of September, up from the previous period and a rebound from a three-year low, according to official Chinese data. That is below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, and the artificial intelligence boom helped lift exports along the way.

Underneath the headline number, property is still the drag. Property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months compared with the same period a year earlier, and the economy has struggled to shake off a long-running property slump that followed years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers. The rebound and the slump are, for now, happening side by side.

sources.title: Rocket Report: FAA eyes more Starbase traffic; India's Skyroot snares US customer

discussion.body: The pairing is the interesting part: a California company selling the idea of extra sunlight buying rides from an Indian launch provider. One of those rockets has already been to orbit — the Vikram-1 made Skyroot the first private Indian firm to manage it in July. Launch is looking less parochial than it used to.

Note the asymmetry in the order. One ride is on the Vikram-1 with that July orbital flight behind it; the other is on the upgraded Vikram-1U. If your product is reflected sunlight, the mirrors are the dream and the rocket manifest is the actual business.

items.title: A Startup Chasing On-Demand Sunlight Buys Two Rides From India's Skyroot
items.body: California-based Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on demand with in-space mirrors, announced Wednesday the purchase of two launches from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace, Payload Space reports. One of the launches will use Skyroot's Vikram-1 rocket, which became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit in July. The other will fly on an upgraded rocket called the Vikram-1U.

sources.title: Jesse Eisenberg Says He ‘Couldn’t Get Movie Studio Parts Anymore’ After Winning a Razzie for ‘Batman v Superman’: ‘The Industry Did Not Want Me to Be in a Superhero Movie’

discussion.body: By Eisenberg's own description of the job, there is no plateau — you're either on the treadmill running up or you're yesterday's news. That makes this less a story about one trophy than about a treadmill, and the Razzie may just have given him a date on the calendar.

The award was also unusually specific: a worst supporting actor Razzie for playing the villain opposite Henry Cavill and Ben Affleck. And his takeaway — no more superhero films — treats the industry's verdict as information rather than as a dare. That's either self-awareness or surrender, and I'm not sure the difference matters to a career.

items.title: Jesse Eisenberg Says a Razzie Cost Him Studio Roles, So He Turned to Directing
items.body: Jesse Eisenberg says he was frozen out of studio movies after winning a Razzie for Zack Snyder's Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice. The mechanism, as he described it during a screen talk at the BFI London Film Festival: he couldn't get into movie studio parts anymore because he had won a Raspberry Award for the Batman movie, and he saw where that was heading. The award — supposedly lighthearted — damaged his acting career, he said, and pushed him to step back from acting and lean into writing and directing. His theory of the business is bleaker, and more useful, than the anecdote: the industry tells you what it wants from you.

sources.title: Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know

discussion.body: Musk's sentence is the strange one. He says the U.S. government is responsible for the system and that speed and usage limits are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately the president. On that account Ukraine isn't really in a fight with a company — it's in a fight with a chain of command.

Zelenskyy's claim is narrower and more concrete than that: SpaceX imposed the restrictions in response to a message from the American government. That is a claim about an instruction being sent, and Trump's denial that he interfered doesn't answer whether one was.

items.title: Three Versions of Who Restricted Ukraine's Starshield Access
items.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. officials remain at odds over disruptions to a key satellite communications service used by the Ukrainian military. Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that he believes the U.S. government is behind his military's loss of normal access to the Starshield and Starlink services, claiming that SpaceX imposed the restrictions in response to a message from the American government. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's version doesn't dispute government control so much as relocate it: he said on X that the U.S. government is responsible for the system, and that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately the president. President Trump, speaking to reporters on Friday, denied interfering with Starshield. Read together, the accounts converge on something the argument obscures — whoever touched the switch, it is described as sitting in Washington. Zelenskyy describes an instruction sent to a contractor; Musk describes a dial owned by the military and the president; Trump describes his own hands. The fight is over what was done, not over who has the power to do it.

sources.title: Sudbury artist who created temporary Jesus head sculpture 10 years ago has risen above the furor

discussion.body: The comedy here is material science. A stopgap sculpted in clay and left outdoors was always likely to lose to rain, and it lost in the most humiliating way available: it dissolved and stained the marble it had been installed to dignify. A repair that damages the thing it repairs is a special kind of failure.

The ending is stranger than the joke, though. The marble head came back and slid straight into anonymity — nobody names a statue for its original nose. The failed substitute is the one still in the artist's possession, still carrying a name. The stopgap outlived its replacement in memory, which is not how restoration is supposed to work.

items.title: The Temporary Jesus Head Was Never Meant to Be the Final Fix
items.body: A decade ago, artist Heather Wise made a clay head to fix a vandalized statue at a local church. It was never meant to be the final fix, but it attracted attention right away, and it has come to be known ever since as the Temporary Jesus Head incident — a name that outlasted the object. The furor put Sudbury, Ont., on the international map for a time. The head itself had a short run: when the clay started to dissolve in the rain, staining the marble, it was returned to Wise, who still has it. The statue's original marble head was eventually returned to the church and re-attached, and the furor died down.

sources.title: Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks

discussion.body: The sentence carrying the real weight is the one about weapons that alter course in flight. Interception is a bet placed on a predicted path, so a drone that keeps revising its own path turns the defender's arithmetic into guesswork rather than a simple question of how many interceptors you have. That is why 'posing a challenge to interceptors' is not filler phrasing.

Announcing support is the easy part; assembling a coalition is the hard part. The Saudi defense minister was meeting the UAE president about strengthening cooperation, according to the UAE's news agency WAM — but those two countries have had tense relations in the recent past, having backed different factions in the Yemeni coalition fighting the rebels. 'Strengthening cooperation' is doing an enormous amount of diplomatic work in that sentence.

items.title: Egypt's Top Security Body Agrees to Support Saudi Arabia Against Houthi Attacks
items.body: Egypt's top security body said it has agreed to support close ally Saudi Arabia in the major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, which the AP describes as the latest front in the Iran war. Saudi Arabia has been pressing allies for military assistance, and the Houthis have repeatedly attacked airports and oil infrastructure across the kingdom with drones and missiles that can change direction during flight — a capability the AP says poses a challenge to interceptors.

sources.title: What does a White House press secretary do?

discussion.body: The credential is almost beside the point next to the job's real bind. Former Pentagon press secretary John Kirby told NPR that the press secretary answers to the public as well as to the president — you have to know what the president is thinking about on any policy issue, and you are also accountable to the American people. Nobody has written an exam for that, which is probably why the job doesn't come with one.

The job may be described in terms of access and accountability, but its memorable moments come from a different instinct. Sean Spicer regularly sparred with members of the media, and while being challenged about the size of the crowds at Trump's inauguration, he told reporters that 'sometimes we can disagree with the facts.' No credential — bar exam or otherwise — protects a podium from that impulse.

items.title: The White House Press Secretary Job Has No Job Description and No Required Qualifications
items.body: The person who speaks for the president of the United States does the job with no job description, no required qualifications and no vetting by Congress. As NPR lays it out, the role isn't designated by Congress either; it rests on nearly a century of presidential custom and tradition instead. That's the whole architecture: a podium, a press corps, and a president who decides how much you get to know. Everything else is improvisation, which is exactly what makes the credential question so revealing. The most recent press secretary found out, as NPR puts it, that you can be fired from the position just as quickly as you were hired. Katie Zacharia was fired last week. What earned her extra scrutiny was describing herself as a lawyer; it was eventually revealed that she had failed the California bar exam, which meant she was not an attorney.

sources.title: Alberta and Québec referendums test Canadian unity amid hostility from the U.S.

discussion.body: In Alberta the referendum is also an internal party instrument. Premier Danielle Smith announced the two-option vote in a bid to unite her divided United Conservative Party, and polls show some 70 per cent of people in Alberta and Québec favour remaining in Canada. That's not a mandate for leaving; it's a lever.

Québec's version was never a party-management exercise. The Parti Québécois has held two independence referendums across three stints in government, and the 1995 vote was decided 50.6 to 49.4. A movement with a near-miss like that in its history doesn't need a unity crisis to keep the question alive.

items.title: Alberta's Referendum and Québec's Independence Ambitions Have Little in Common
items.body: Albertans are voting on whether to stay in Canada or begin a process toward a binding independence referendum. By 2030, people in Québec could face a similar choice. Set the two movements side by side and the resemblance stops early. Beyond a shared interest in more autonomy from the federal government, Alberta and Québec have little in common. Alberta's grievances are about federal economic, energy and climate policy, immigration and political representation. Québec's are about protecting a distinctive language and culture in an anglo-dominated North America. One is a fight over who writes the rules; the other is a fight over whether a culture survives.

sources.title: Blue Origin is going all in on the New Glenn rocket

discussion.body: Two extra catch ships is the telling line. Pads are real estate; snagging a returning booster is a logistical habit, and the plan treats it as routine enough to need a fleet rather than a single vessel.

Routine is the aspiration, not the record. That hundred-plus figure arrives dressed in 'intent' and 'eventually'. The fair reading of a facilities expansion is capacity built to chase a cadence, not evidence that the cadence has arrived.

items.title: For 100+ Flights a Year, Blue Origin Is Buying Pads and Booster-Catching Ships
items.body: Blue Origin announced an expansion of its Florida launch facilities with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there. The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. It also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of New Glenn; it currently has one, named Jacklyn. Notice which hardware the plan leans on. More pads mean more places to launch, and more catch ships mean more capacity to recover what comes back down. If a hundred-plus flights a year is the target, the recovery side and the ground side have to scale with it, and this announcement spends on both. It is a plan as the company describes it, framed as intent rather than a demonstrated cadence.

sources.title: Wall Street Expectations for Treasury Yields: Higher for Longer

discussion.body: The concession worth noticing isn't a number, it's the phrase: assumptions about demand. Missing on growth or inflation is a forecast miss. Concluding that you misjudged the appetite for a government's debt is a different kind of miss, and it's the one that keeps a spread from 3.95% to 5.63% alive.

Or that spread is just what a survey's low and high look like: two named forecasters at the extremes, pointed at December 2027 rather than at anything checkable next quarter. The solid part of the report is the direction and its three stated reasons — growth, inflation, and the fiscal trajectory.

items.title: Why Treasury Yields Climbed on Growth, Inflation and Fiscal Worry — and Why the Rethink Was Demand
items.body: Treasury yields have climbed since the start of the summer. In the October Wall Street Journal survey of economists that Econbrowser relays, the reported cause is a three-part mix: improving growth, new inflationary pressures and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory. Many of the surveyed economists said that cocktail forced them to re-evaluate their assumptions about investors' demand for Treasurys — a question about who wants to hold the debt, not just about the level of a rate. Econbrowser's chart tracks ten-year Treasury yields alongside the October and July survey means, all in percent. The disagreement is wide: the low prediction for December 2027 is 3.95% and the high is 5.63%, from James Smith and Allen Sinai respectively — roughly 1.7 points apart. One relationship makes the debate legible. Yields rise when prices fall, so weaker appetite for a bond does not announce itself as a discount; it arrives as a higher yield. Read that way, the fiscal-trajectory worry and the demand question are the same conversation.

sources.title: Macron condemns those who 'sought to bring down the Republic' after rioting mars nationwide protests

discussion.body: Macron's language separates the protests' stated grievances—living costs, school conditions—from the disorder blamed on far-left elements.

But the blame isn't only coming from the Élysée. Marine Le Pen called Macron's government “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” while Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march, insisted that “those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.” Le Pen uses the unrest to attack the government; Mélenchon tries to keep the protest separate from the looting.

items.title: Macron Denounces 'Insurrectionist Elements' as France's Riot Arrests Top 2,400
items.body: French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public's “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested. Macron echoed other government officials in blaming much of the violence on far-left activists, accusing them of attacking police and public buildings to foment chaos, and he denounced “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.” He had earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked city halls in several cities.

sources.title: What does it really take to be a resilient mother?

discussion.body: The portfolio framing locates resilience in the combination of strengths and supports. That shifts the focus from the individual alone to the structures around her.
The harder shift may be in meaning-making: if a woman's identity came from achievement, early motherhood's request to “just stand still” isn't rest—it's a loss of the self she knew.

items.title: Why New Motherhood Can Dismantle a 'Resilience Portfolio'
items.body: The psychologist Sherry Hamby and colleagues propose a “resilience portfolio” model. Grounded in research on adverse experiences, it describes how a person's physical and mental health outcomes after adversity might depend on the combination of their strengths and support structures—their portfolio. For many women, new motherhood seems to almost systematically dismantle the portfolio of strengths they previously relied on, starting with the domain of meaning-making. Women the author speaks to are often used to defining themselves through achievement and getting things done, but early motherhood, in a sense, asks them to just stand still.

discussion.body: The transferable lesson is not that some particular paper lied. It is the report-in-isolation problem, which the writer names from experience as a science journalist: each study gets published as its own headline, weighed against nothing else we know, and a reader has no way to see the pile it is actually sitting on.

Read the review's wording closely, though. "Does not clearly link" is not a clean bill of health; it is a statement about what the collected evidence shows, which is a narrower thing than an all-clear. And the cost the writer identifies is concrete: by the time the synthesis landed, countless women had been needlessly scared about a painkiller widely considered one of the safest to take during pregnancy. Getting the synthesis later is not the same as getting it before the fear spread.

items.title: A Paracetamol Warning, Then a Review That Better Represented the Evidence
items.body: A couple of months after the US Food and Drug Administration announced it would add a warning label to the painkiller acetaminophen (paracetamol), claiming that taking the drug during pregnancy increased a child's risk of autism, researchers published a major review that better represented the full body of knowledge. Its conclusion: "Existing evidence does not clearly link maternal paracetamol use during pregnancy with autism or ADHD in offspring." The writer who reported on the announcement argues the FDA and its parent health department cherry-picked a few studies and downplayed more robust findings. Put the two documents side by side and the difference is structural: one claim built from a selected handful of papers, one attempt to weigh everything that existed.
